opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, because the tools only help if people trust them for the right reasons. When I first joined the team, there were two camps. Some engineers treated the model like an oracle: if it said a setup change would gain a tenth on a lap, they'd run with it. Others wouldn't touch it at all because it felt like a black box. Both reactions come from the same place, which is not really understanding what the model is doing under the hood.

So I spent a lot of time just sitting with people: race engineers, strategists, even some of the mechanics. I walked them through how these models learn patterns from data, why they can sound very confident and still be wrong, and where they tend to be strong versus where they're guessing. Once people understood that the model is basically a very fast pattern-matcher that's only as good as the data and the question you give it, everything changed. They started asking better questions. They started cross-checking outputs against telemetry instead of taking them at face value. And they started spotting the cases where the model was out of its depth, like an unusual track condition or a weather situation we didn't have much history on.

What makes it so impactful is that it scales in a way my own work doesn't. I can build one tool, but if I help thirty people understand how to use AI well, that judgment shows up in hundreds of decisions across a race weekend that I'm never going to be in the room for. In racing, the margins are tiny and the decisions happen fast. Having a team that knows when to lean on the model and when to override it is worth more than any single model I could build.

r001.rationale: The response explains how learning that models find patterns in data helps the team understand when and how to use them effectively, including asking better questions and checking outputs.

r002.rationale: It says models are only as good as the question users give them and describes people learning to ask better questions, assigning users responsibility for the input.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, when I joined the team, the thing that struck me wasn't a lack of tools. We had plenty of models, dashboards, simulation outputs, predictive stuff for tire degradation and strategy calls. What we didn't have was a shared understanding of what those models were actually doing underneath. And in racing, that gap is dangerous, because decisions get made in seconds on the pit wall, and if someone treats a model output as gospel when it's really a probability with wide error bars, you lose races. Or worse, you lose trust in the whole system after one bad call.

So I started doing these short sessions, sometimes just twenty minutes, with engineers, strategists, even some of the mechanics. Not teaching them to build models. Teaching them how a model gets trained, what it's seen and what it hasn't, why it might be confident and wrong, what overfitting looks like in practice. Things like: this degradation model has basically never seen a wet-to-dry crossover at this circuit, so when it gives you a number there, discount it heavily.

What surprised me was how fast that changed the conversations. People stopped asking "what does the model say" and started asking "what does the model know." Strategists began pushing back on outputs in a really informed way. Engineers started flagging edge cases before they bit us. And the data science side got better feedback, because the people using the tools finally spoke enough of the language to say precisely where things were breaking.

I think the reason I rate it above almost anything else I've done technically is leverage. A better model helps you in the situations it covers. A team that understands models helps you in every situation, including the ones nobody anticipated. That's the one that compounds.

r001.rationale: The response says teaching how models are trained and what they have and have not seen helps the team interpret outputs, question them, and use them effectively.

r002.rationale: The response describes users questioning outputs and flagging edge cases, but does not say they are responsible for identifying the input that will elicit a desired output.

astra-6.text:
Because a model is only useful if people know how to work with it. In a racing team, you’re making decisions under pressure, so you need to understand what an AI tool can help with, where it might be wrong, and when to bring your own judgment to bear.

For me, education helps people move from either trusting it blindly or dismissing it entirely to asking better questions. What information is it using? How do we check the result? Is this the right tool for the problem? When that understanding spreads across the team, the impact goes beyond any single application. You give people the confidence to find useful applications themselves.

r001.rationale: The response discusses understanding what AI can help with and where it may be wrong, but does not explain how understanding how models are built helps people work with them effectively.

r002.rationale: The response encourages asking questions and checking results, but does not assign users responsibility for identifying the input needed to get their desired output.

sol-6.1.text:
Because a model only becomes useful to the team when people understand how to work with it. You can build something technically impressive, but if the people making decisions don’t understand what it’s telling them, where it’s uncertain, or when to question it, its impact is limited.

Education helps people connect the model to their own expertise. They can ask better questions, spot when an output doesn’t make sense, and give feedback that improves what we build. In racing, where decisions often have to happen quickly, that shared understanding is incredibly valuable. You’re helping the whole team make better use of the technology.

r001.rationale: The response discusses understanding how to work with a model, but does not explain that understanding how models are built makes them easier to conceptualize.

r002.rationale: It says education helps people ask better questions, but does not clearly assign users responsibility for identifying inputs that will elicit their desired output.
